rv.q: Either way, her life is intense, complicated, imperfect yet thrilling — as is If/Then itself.
In this intelligent, surprising, altogether original new musical, the main character is a 39-year-old divorced woman, Elizabeth, who returns to New York after 12 years as a wife in Phoenix.
But a show with so much potential is marred by poor editing.
The great strength of Menzel's performance in this major new musical of generational shift is that she makes you feel like she doesn't fully buy into either explanation.
It remains something of a conundrum, for the conceit comes across, even now, less as a scintillating invention than as an encumbrance.
Too bad she’s not in a show worthy of her talents.
Menzel carries the show but can't force us to care about Liz/Beth's average life choices.
The musical's central conceit — exploring how life might unfold differently based on seemingly small choices — is intriguing, but the execution feels more dutiful than inspired.
All that's visible is the finished product, a piece of storytelling as plain and true and beautiful as a well-laid brick wall.
Taken together, they feel less like variations on a theme than dogged reiterations of a theme.
This smaller-than-life show can’t extinguish Menzel’s larger-than-life persona, but it certainly diminishes her Amazonian strengths as a performer.
Menzel's performance is nothing short of extraordinary, showcasing her remarkable vocal range and emotional depth
But the show’s exploration of fate and chance seldom rises above Hallmark-card sentimentality — and the characters have no more depth.

"As one of the few new musicals not based on a familiar film or pop song catalog (or anything else for that matter), "If/Then" certainly is a breath of fresh air. And despite nagging issues with its overall concept and divided story lines, it is a smart, romantic piece with a well-crafted soft rock score and great performances all around...
Menzel attacking a high note has all the high-voltage charm of a jackhammer going after reinforced concrete.
One of the best crafted scenes and songs - 'The Moment Explodes' - will brings gasps
That may be all well and good, but that point gets clouded in confusing storylines.
Menzel's powerhouse vocals and magnetic stage presence help compensate for some of the show's shortcomings
If/Then has its moments, but it is a letdown after Kitt and Yorkey's electrifying achievement with Next to Normal.
If Menzel wasn’t around with her big belt and mellow warmth, there would be no reason to visit at all.
Even she cannot save the bifurcated and bipolar If/Then.
